items.title: 9.5 Ethical, Legal, and Environmental Impacts of Computing

source_refs.note: Topic 9.5 with its Do You Know, Class Activity and Tidbit (PDF 135-137); no book figure, so the impacts figure is original and the laws are carried as a table. Added: where GDPR applies and that PECA was amended in 2025, both to be reviewed. Short Q7-9 and Long Q7-8 are answered here.

blocks.text: Computing affects daily life in many ways: it can have ethical or unethical effects, legal or illegal consequences, and an impact on the environment. Ethical use means fair, responsible choices; legal use follows the laws on technology; and environmental impact includes energy use and electronic waste. Awareness of these helps people make informed, responsible decisions.

Ethical use means acting responsibly and avoiding harm: respecting privacy and fairness and handling information properly, while considering the effects of decisions on people, organisations and society.

blocks.title: Do you know?
blocks.text: Copying online content without permission can break both copyright law and digital ethics.

items: Intellectual property: creations of the mind, such as software, music, books, images, videos, designs and inventions, legally owned by people or organisations. Respect it by not copying, sharing or using work without permission, and by giving credit.
Data ownership: the right to control personal information. Personal and sensitive data must be protected and not misused.
Unethical behaviour: hacking, spreading false information and cyberbullying cause harm, damage reputations and can bring legal penalties; even small online actions can have big effects.

blocks.text: Legal aspects and data privacy laws

Legal aspects of computing are the rules that govern technology and digital information. Cybercrime is illegal activity using computers, networks or the Internet, such as hacking, identity theft and online fraud. Laws protect individuals, organisations and society from misuse of data, and data privacy laws make sure personal and sensitive information is collected, stored and shared responsibly.

blocks.caption: Two important laws
rows: Rules on how organisations collect, store and use personal data; requires transparency and consent, and gives people the right to access or delete their data. Many countries and companies follow similar standards.

The main law against cybercrime, protecting individuals, organisations and the state; covers hacking, identity theft, online fraud and unauthorised access to data, with legal penalties. Organisations must also follow data-protection policies.

blocks.title: Class activity
blocks.text: Using a guided worksheet, list the cybercrimes covered by PECA.

Computing uses energy, produces electronic waste (e-waste) and contributes to pollution, while also shaping communication, behaviour and culture. E-waste is discarded devices such as old computers, phones, batteries, printers and chargers; dumping or burning it releases harmful substances that damage the environment and health. Sustainable computing means using, designing and disposing of technology so as to reduce harm: reduce (keep devices longer, choose energy-efficient ones), reuse (repair, donate) and recycle through proper e-waste collectors.

blocks.title: Tidbit
blocks.text: Recycling, reusing and using energy-efficient devices reduce harm to the environment.

Technology changes how people communicate, work and find information: social media, digital learning and online services shape culture and daily life, and improve education, healthcare and business. It can also create problems, such as the digital divide between people with and without access, and loss of privacy. Understanding these effects encourages thoughtful, responsible use.
